title: ThreadX 5.6 → current 6.x
subtitle: Cortex-M4 → modern Cortex-M, with executable evidence

blocks.text: A reproducible Clang + QEMU proof, not a promise of a full WICED board conversion.

rows: Compiled and linked only; no M85 runtime claim

blocks.text: Start with the OS/core differences, then inspect the code changes and measured results. Use ← / →, touch arrows, or swipe. Home returns here.

title: ThreadX 5 and 6: what actually changes
subtitle: Same RTOS service concepts, different source / port / licensing baseline

rows: Public common C source + CPU/toolchain ports
Same service families; retest semantics and configuration
Pinned release contains M4, M55 and M85 ports
Current selected release has MIT license
Vendor SDK and old GNU build
Rebuilt source, matching ABI, Clang + CMake

blocks.text: This is an evidence-based comparison of the supplied SDK, not a claim that every ThreadX 5 distribution had identical ports or rights. Kernel source is absent from the historical SDK.

title: Why choose current 6.x for this project?
subtitle: Remove the opaque binary / port dependency before changing the core

items: We need source we can rebuild for the target ABI and freely share.
The selected current release includes an upstream Cortex-M85 port.
A pinned open source baseline enables review, regression tests and reproducible build evidence.
Later 6.x versions include fixes and port updates; audit relevant release notes, do not freeze at the linked 2022 tag.
An old licensed TX5 kernel could theoretically be custom-ported. That is different scope, risk and rights.

blocks.text: A version number alone does not make a product faster, secure, certified or production-ready. 6.x is the practical source/port/licensing baseline for THIS public PoC.

title: The exact version, not a moving branch
subtitle: The linked 6.1.12 release is not the latest release

rows: Current selected release: MIT; preserve upstream notices

blocks.text: Do not swap in the older tag while assuming its checked-in license text is the same. The old tag contains hardware-linked Azure RTOS licensing language.

title: Cortex-M4, M55 and M85
subtitle: Keep CPU architecture distinct from a particular microcontroller

blocks.text: Core IP features and SoC implementations vary. A new core does not bring the old STM32F4 GPIO, clocks, memory addresses, DMA or board wiring with it.

title: Compatibility stops at the hardware boundary
subtitle: Portable C is only one layer of an RTOS migration

items: Recompile all RTOS-facing code and control blocks; never relink a CM4 binary on the strength of API names.
Match CPU, Thumb ISA, float ABI, kernel flags and stack alignment across every translation unit.
Verify exception return, PSP/MSP context, IRQ priorities and SysTick routing.
Plan the SoC linker map, VTOR, caches/TCM, MPU, TrustZone and DMA coherency separately.
Test FPU/MVE task switching and security state on real M85 hardware before claiming those paths.

blocks.text:
-mcpu=cortex-m4   # same-release control build
-mcpu=cortex-m55  # executable QEMU proof
-mcpu=cortex-m85  # compile/link proof only
# common: --target=arm-none-eabi -mthumb -mfloat-abi=hard
blocks.label: Compiler target change, not a complete BSP port

title: The most modern runnable QEMU Cortex-M here
subtitle: Probe the installed executable instead of relying on development docs

blocks.text:
qemu-system-arm --version
qemu-system-arm -machine help
qemu-system-arm -cpu help
# installed: 11.1.0
# present: mps3-an547 / cortex-m55
# absent:  mps3-an555 / cortex-m85
blocks.label: Actual local inventory, saved in evidence/qemu-*.txt

blocks.text: M55 is the newest Cortex-M CPU exposed by this installed QEMU build. QEMU development documentation mentions AN555, but it is not available in the tested binary.
We never run an M85 image under an M55 CPU and label it M85. The M85 ELF remains a separate, explicitly unexecuted build artifact.

title: Licensing is an engineering input
subtitle: Public GitHub visibility does not imply permission to redistribute

items: The supplied GPIO .c and .mk files explicitly carry proprietary Broadcom notices.
The SDK README says its ThreadX / NetX objects are free for WICED use only.
No proprietary GPIO file, TX5 archive, Wi-Fi firmware or restricted vendor stack is included.
The new demo is independently written to preserve the LED/button behavior.
Original work uses MIT; the pinned ThreadX source retains its upstream MIT license.
PDF typography embeds open-source Roboto fonts under OFL 1.1, with notices shipped beside the PDF.
Clang and QEMU are external tools, not firmware components relicensed as MIT.

blocks.text: This proves the migration approach on shareable code. It does not claim the complete old WICED SDK is OSS or that a technical audit replaces legal review.

title: Upgrade in separate dimensions
subtitle: Avoid attributing an OS change to a CPU change

blocks.name: workflow
blocks.caption: Control: ThreadX 6 on M4. New runtime proof: same ThreadX 6 on M55. M85: same source, separate port build.

blocks.text: The TX5 reference is a behavior/source-inventory baseline, not a runnable benchmark baseline. Separating the dimensions makes the remaining hardware work visible.

title: What really executes
subtitle: No mock RTOS, no fake emulator success

blocks.name: architecture
blocks.caption: Clang-built ARM firmware uses real ThreadX scheduler and service code under QEMU.

blocks.text: The board adapter virtualizes two LEDs and deterministic active-low buttons. It does not emulate or access a physical GPIO controller.

title: Diff 1: RTOS delivery and build
subtitle: A conceptual integration diff, not copied proprietary SDK code

blocks.text:
- RTOS input: opaque ThreadX.ARM_CM4.release.a
- Toolchain: vendor SDK make + legacy GNU assumptions
+ RTOS input: pinned third_party/threadx/common + selected CPU port
+ add_subdirectory(third_party/threadx)
+ target_link_libraries(threadx_gpio_demo PRIVATE threadx)
+ Clang C + integrated assembler + LLD
+ --target=arm-none-eabi -mcpu=<selected core>
blocks.label: Build-layer migration, representative rather than an applied WICED patch

blocks.text: Source rebuild avoids mixing TX5 headers with TX6 object layouts. Kernel configuration comes from a single tx_user.h shared by the library and application.

title: Diff 2: task lifecycle is explicit
subtitle: Initialize static objects before allowing the scheduler to run

blocks.label: Representative lifecycle diff; implementation checks every creation status

items: Lower numeric priority is higher priority in ThreadX.
Stack storage is static and aligned as ULONG; lifetime exceeds the task.
Application and RTOS objects are freshly compiled, not ABI-reused.

title: Diff 3: milliseconds versus RTOS ticks
subtitle: Keep units visible; avoid a silent tenfold or hundredfold delay error

blocks.text:
- delay API accepts 250 milliseconds
+ #define TX_TIMER_TICKS_PER_SECOND 100
+ #define LED_UPDATE_TICKS 25U
+ tx_thread_sleep(LED_UPDATE_TICKS);   // 250 ms virtual time
+ SysTick reload = DEMO_CLOCK_HZ / 100 - 1
+ SysTick_Handler -> _tx_timer_interrupt
blocks.label: Timing integration diff, plus a measured tick invariant

blocks.text: The tested board clock constants are 25 MHz for MPS2-M4 and 32 MHz for MPS3-M55. The M85 build reuses the demonstration map/clock; a real M85 SoC must replace them.
QEMU icount is synthetic: 128 ns per emulated instruction. The tick invariant is a scheduler test, not a physical time or jitter guarantee.

title: Diff 4: preserve the held-button latch
subtitle: A subtle behavioral detail, checked at release as well as press

blocks.label: Actual correction in the new application, not a TX5 kernel diff

blocks.text: The reference behavior pauses the toggle latch while the button is held. An implementation that merely sets the latch true while held changes the release behavior.
The verifier deliberately rejects a cycle-4 OFF result.

title: Diff 5: startup assembly under Clang
subtitle: A real encountered failure, with a trace-supported fix

blocks.text:
- sub r2, r2, r1   // Clang emitted sub.w, without updating flags
- beq copy_done    // branches on stale flags
- sub r2, r2, #1   // same hidden flag dependency
- bne copy_loop    // loop fails to terminate
+ copy_loop:
+     cmp r1, r2   // explicit end-pointer comparison
+     bhs copy_done
+     ldrb r3, [r0], #1
+     strb r3, [r1], #1
+     b copy_loop
blocks.label: Compared to the current MIT upstream example startup, not Broadcom source

blocks.text: QEMU traced a precise bus fault at 0x00080000 during the endless startup copy. The replacement has explicit comparisons, copies .data, clears .bss, and enables CP10/CP11.
Changing compiler is not just changing an executable name. Assembly flag semantics need testing.

title: Diff 6: one security mode and one ABI
subtitle: Scope down the first proof; make omitted features explicit

blocks.text:
+ // include/tx_user.h: compiled into kernel AND application
+ #define TX_SINGLE_MODE_SECURE
+ #define TX_TIMER_TICKS_PER_SECOND 100
+ #define TX_ENABLE_STACK_CHECKING
+ // no secure/non-secure task transitions in this demo
+ // use hard-float ABI consistently; enable CP10/CP11 at reset
blocks.label: Actual demonstrator configuration

items: Single-secure avoids falsely exercising secure-stack allocation paths without a non-secure image.
Hard-float compile/link is established; dedicated mixed FPU/MVE context stress remains pending.
SVC is unused in this configuration; PendSV handles context switching.
Do not infer a TrustZone security policy from a successful boot.

title: Diff 7: IRQ, vectors and memory belong to the BSP
subtitle: Minimal executable map now; production SoC map later

blocks.text:
+ .vectors: initial MSP, Reset, faults, PendSV, SysTick
+ VTOR = address of demo_vectors
+ PendSV priority = 0xff; SysTick priority = 0x40
+ CODE: 0x00000000, 512 KiB
+ RAM:  0x20000000, 32 KiB
+ system stack: 2048 bytes, 8-byte aligned
+ linker ASSERT: reserved RAM must fit
blocks.label: boards/qemu.ld + src/startup.S + src/tx_initialize_low_level.c

blocks.text: These are demonstrator settings, not a claimed M85 board port. A Cortex-M85 core can appear in SoCs with different memory, clocks, controllers and IRQ routing.

title: Diff 8: success becomes a checked contract
subtitle: Fail on missing, wrong or partial output

blocks.text:
- visually inspect a blinking LED and assume migration works
+ verify CPUID part number and RTOS version
+ require queue / event / semaphore / mutex / pool self-test PASS
+ check all 10 button + LED rows
+ require 9 intervals of exactly 25 virtual ticks
+ require explicit completion and QEMU exit status 0
+ reject timeout, wrong identity, wrong state or partial log
blocks.label: tests/run_qemu.py + 11 verifier unit tests

blocks.text: One positive verifier fixture plus ten deliberately corrupted fixtures pass their expected assertions. The firmware's real run is tested separately through CTest.

title: The RTOS services really switch tasks
subtitle: A higher-priority worker must suspend, resume and signal

blocks.label: Condensed from the independently written service self-test

items: Worker creation preempts the LED task; an empty queue suspends the worker.
Sending the payload resumes the worker; the event proves execution reached the receiver.
The timer wakes the sleeping LED task nine times through the real ThreadX timer path.
Mutex and pool checks are basic operations, not exhaustive contention/fragmentation stress.

title: Replay the verified LED run
subtitle: Recorded QEMU evidence, not a browser-side ARM emulator

blocks.text: Two buttons are scripted active-low inputs. Buttons force their paired LED on while held; the paused toggle resumes after release. Step through cycles 0–9.
The replay data is embedded from evidence/m55-run.json, after the host verifier accepted it.

title: Memory chart: linked ROM
subtitle: Clang -O3; same RTOS release, same app and service tests

blocks.text: No TX5 size delta is claimed. These are actual ELF sections for this instrumented workload, not marketing estimates or minimum kernel footprints.

title: Memory chart: reserved RAM
subtitle: Include stacks and test infrastructure, not only global data

blocks.name: ram
blocks.caption: RAM = .data + .bss + 2 KiB system stack. Static task stacks are already inside .bss.

blocks.text: The M4 and M55 runtime report sizeof(TX_THREAD) = 180 bytes in this build configuration. That observation is not permission to treat every TX5 or differently configured TCB as ABI-compatible.

title: Stack headroom is measured, not assumed
subtitle: Useful early evidence; not production stack qualification

blocks.name: stack
blocks.caption: Observed LED thread stack high-water under the test workload; 1024 bytes reserved.

blocks.text: Values are ThreadX stack-check samples. Production worst-case paths, nested interrupts, FPU/MVE context and M85 behavior still require stress and hardware validation.

title: Performance chart: emulator test cost
subtitle: Measure what was actually run, and state what the number means

blocks.name: host-cost
blocks.caption: Eight alternating QEMU runs per core on this Windows host, using deterministic icount.

blocks.text: These host durations include launch, TCG, virtual sleeps, self-tests and console I/O. They do not measure M4/M55 throughput, context-switch cycles, interrupt latency or M85 speed.

title: Histogram: repeatability of the host harness
subtitle: Samples are retained, not reduced to an unexplained mean

blocks.name: host-histogram
blocks.caption: Every plotted sample is in evidence/summary.json.

blocks.text: Use this to budget an automated test job and spot test-host variability. Do not turn the median difference into a CPU performance claim.

title: Histogram: scheduler timing contract
subtitle: 144 measured intervals, all at the requested 25 ticks

blocks.name: tick-histogram
blocks.caption: 8 runs × 9 intervals × 2 cores = 144 intervals, all 25 virtual ticks.

blocks.text: The 100 Hz tick gives 250 ms in the configured virtual-time model. Tick quantization and synthetic instruction time cannot establish physical sub-tick jitter.

title: What the M85 build proves
subtitle: Correct target attributes and resolved symbols, not execution

blocks.text:
llvm-readelf -A build/m85/threadx_gpio_demo.elf
CPU_name: cortex-m85
CPU_arch: ARM v8.1-M Mainline
ABI_VFP_args: AAPCS VFP
MVE_arch: MVE integer and float
llvm-nm --undefined-only build/m85/threadx_gpio_demo.elf
# no undefined symbols
blocks.label: Actual attribute inspection; build uses upstream ports/cortex_m85/gnu

blocks.text: This establishes that Clang compiled and LLD linked the application with the M85 port. The demo linker/clock are not a production M85 SoC definition.
There is no M85 runtime, performance, power, PACBTI or mixed FPU/MVE correctness result.

title: The hardware acceptance gate
subtitle: Turn this PoC into a product migration with explicit tests

rows: Vendor-approved startup, linker map, GPIO polarity, clock tree, IRQ map
Stress preemption + nested IRQ + mixed scalar/FPU/MVE tasks; inspect saved context
TrustZone policy, secure gateways/stacks, MPU and optional PACBTI configuration
On-silicon cycles, IRQ latency distribution, deadline/WCET, throughput and energy
Regression suite for peripheral, network, watchdog and low-power interactions
Licensing, SBOM, safety/change-impact assessment, traceable requirements

blocks.text: The LED PoC reduces feasibility risk. It is not a claim that Wi-Fi, TLS, OTA, safety certification or all application deadlines have migrated.

title: Reproduce the result
subtitle: Public source, pinned dependency, raw evidence and automated checks

blocks.text:
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/zuwasi/TX5-upgrade.git
cd TX5-upgrade
cmake --preset m4 && cmake --build --preset m4
cmake --preset m55 && cmake --build --preset m55
cmake --preset m85 && cmake --build --preset m85
ctest --test-dir build/m4 --output-on-failure
ctest --test-dir build/m55 --output-on-failure
python -m unittest discover -s tests -p test_verifier.py -v
python scripts/collect_evidence.py --repeats 8
blocks.label: Tools: Clang/LLVM, LLD, CMake, Ninja, Python and ARM QEMU

blocks.text: The GitHub workflow uses a Linux package toolchain, so CI tool versions may differ from the recorded Windows Clang 22.1.3 / QEMU 11.1.0 measurements. Local evidence lists exact versions.
Only run firmware you trust with host semihosting enabled.

title: The technical conclusion
subtitle: A bounded yes, backed by executable evidence

items: YES: the legacy GPIO behavior is implementable on current MIT ThreadX.
YES: the same application and service tests execute on M4 and modern M55 QEMU targets.
YES: Clang compiles and links the same application using the upstream Cortex-M85 port.
NOT YET: M85 runtime and real-board BSP / timing / security qualification.
NEXT: choose the actual M85 SoC and run the hardware acceptance suite.

blocks.text: Approve a hardware migration spike with measurable exit criteria, rather than treating a successful LED demo as a full-product release.
